summary:
Penza Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors and has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and changes to gender markers on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings address LGBT travellers directly.

The UK government country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records that same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the "gay propaganda" law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeat offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. The same note records that at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024, through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

The extremism machinery applies nationwide and reaches any visitor charged within Penza Oblast. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, and that 81 people across 98 court cases since January 2024 had been convicted of administrative offences for displaying those symbols, mostly on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation enabled criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison and built on the 2013 propaganda law; Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Official advisories reflect the risk. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night, The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025). In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Penza Oblast is one administrative unit within this national pattern and operates under the same federal statutes, courts and prosecutorial bodies; no separate oblast-level legal regime for transgender people is sourced here.

The United States places Russia at its highest travel advisory level, Do Not Travel, with explicit warnings for LGBT travellers, while the United Kingdom's asylum authority treats LGBT+ Russians as members of a particular social group entitled to refugee-convention protection. Human Rights Watch's June 2025 call on governments to offer safe haven situates the country among those from which asylum is considered warranted on identity grounds.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Penza Oblast-specific enforcement records, prosecutions or detentions of transgender people are sourced in this inventory; all documented cases cited here occurred in other regions, including Moscow, St Petersburg and the area near Novosibirsk. Whether oblast-level authorities issue guidance or apply additional measures specific to the region is unresolved.

Local conditions inside Penza Oblast are not sourced: detention facility conditions, the presence or absence of LGBT venues, access to legal assistance, and any documented hate violence within the oblast remain unverified here. Reporting on physical coercion rests on a single documented case in another region, so its frequency within Penza Oblast is unresolved.

The date currency of the UK country policy note is unresolved: it is dated June 2025 with a later page update recorded, and this inventory does not confirm whether its factual findings have been revised since. Whether any enforcement action under the extremism designation has been brought in Penza Oblast specifically is not sourced.
